Based on my research, I need to find election years from 1930-2020 that meet **both** criteria:
1. A Democratic president won re-election (serving two full terms) and was succeeded by a Republican president
2. An American female gymnast won the Olympic All-Around Gold medal in that same year

Let me analyze this step-by-step:

## Step 1: Identify Democratic Presidents Who Served Two Full Terms (1930-2020) and Were Succeeded by Republicans

From the search results:
- **Franklin D. Roosevelt**: Won elections in 1932, 1936, 1940, 1944 (4 terms), but was succeeded by **Harry Truman (Democrat)** in 1945
- **Bill Clinton**: Won elections in **1992 and 1996**, serving two full terms, and was succeeded by **George W. Bush (Republican)** in 2000

So the only presidential election year that fits criterion #1 is **1996**.

## Step 2: Check if an American Female Gymnast Won Olympic All-Around Gold in 1996

According to the Olympic results:
- **1996 Atlanta Olympics**: The women's individual all-around gold medal was won by **Lilia Podkopayeva (Ukraine)**, not an American
- American gymnasts at the 1996 Games included Shannon Miller and Dominique Dawes, who competed on the U.S. team (which won team gold), but neither won the individual all-around title

## Step 3: List of ALL American Women's Individual All-Around Gold Medalists

- **1984**: Mary Lou Retton
- **2004**: Carly Patterson  
- **2008**: Nastia Liukin
- **2012**: Gabby Douglas
- **2016**: Simone Biles
- **2020/2021**: Sunisa Lee

None of these years correspond to presidential election years where a Democrat won re-election for two terms and was succeeded by a Republican.

**There are NO US presidential election years from 1930-2020 that satisfy both conditions.** 

While Bill Clinton meets the presidential criteria (democratic president who served two full terms, succeeded by a Republican), the only American female gymnasts to win individual all-around gold medals did so in years (1984, 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020) that do not align with his re-election year of 1996.

Bill Clinton's tenure as the 42nd president of the United States began with his first inauguration on January 20, 1993, and ended on January 20, 2001. Clinton, a Democrat from Arkansas, took office after defeating the Republican incumbent president George H. W. Bush and independent businessman Ross Perot in the 1992 presidential election. Four years later, he won re-election in the 1996 presidential election, after defeating the Republican nominee Bob Dole, and also Perot again (then as the nominee of the Reform Party). Alongside Clinton's presidency, the Democratic Party also held their majorities in the House of Representatives and the Senate during the 103rd U.S. Congress following the 1992 elections, thereby attained an overall federal government trifecta. Clinton was constitutionally limited to two terms (the first re-elected Democrat president to be so) and was succeeded by Republican George W. Bush, who won the 2000 presidential election against Clinton'ds preferred successor, Vice President Al Gore.

President Clinton oversaw the second longest period of peacetime economic expansion[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Bill_Clinton#cite_note-1) in American history. Months into his first term, he signed the Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1993, which raised taxes and set the stage for future budget surpluses. He signed the bipartisan Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act and won ratification of the North American Free Trade Agreement, despite opposition from trade unions and environmentalists. Clinton's most ambitious legislative initiative, a plan to provide universal health care, failed to advance through Congress. A backlash to Clinton's agenda sparked the Republican Revolution, with the GOP taking control of the House of Representatives for the first time in 40 years. Clinton pivoted to the center in response by assembling a bipartisan coalition to pass welfare reform, and he successfully expanded [health insurance for children](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Children's_Health_Insurance_Program "State Children's Health Insurance Program").

While Clinton's economy was strong, his presidency oscillated dramatically from high to low and back again, which historian Gil Troy characterized in six Acts. Act I in early 1993 was "Bush League" with amateurish distractions. By mid-1993 Clinton had recovered to Act II, passing a balanced budget and the NAFTA trade deal. Act III, 1994, saw the Republicans mobilizing under Newt Gingrich, defeating Clinton's healthcare reforms, and taking control of the House of Representatives for the first time in forty years. The years 1995 to 1997 saw the comeback in Act IV, with a triumphant reelection landslide in 1996. However, Act V, the Clinton–Lewinsky scandal and impeachment made 1998 a lost year. Clinton concluded happily with Act VI by deregulating the banking system in 1999.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Bill_Clinton#cite_note-2) In foreign policy, Clinton initiated a bombing campaign in the Balkans, which led to the creation of a United Nations protectorate in Kosovo. He played a major role of the expansion of NATO into former Eastern Bloc countries and remained on positive terms with Russian presidentBoris Yeltsin. During his second term, Clinton presided over the deregulation of the financial and telecommunications industry. Clinton's second term also saw the first federal budget surpluses since the 1960s. The ratio of debt held by the public to GDP fell from 47.8% in 1993 to 33.6% by 2000. His impeachment in 1998 arose after he denied claims of having an affair with a White House intern, Monica Lewinsky under oath. He was acquitted of all charges by the Senate. He appointed Ruth Bader Ginsburg and Stephen Breyer to the U.S. Supreme Court.
With a 66% approval rating at the time he left office, Clinton had the highest exit approval rating of any president since the end of World War II.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Bill_Clinton#cite_note-3) Despite the Clinton–Lewinsky scandal and numerous high-profile controversies, historians and political scientists generally rank Clinton as an above-average president.
1992 Electoral College vote results

Incumbent president George H. W. Bush and President-elect Clinton on November 18, 1992.
President George H. W. Bush's popularity in the aftermath of the successful 1991 Gulf War convinced many prominent Democrats to sit out the 1992 presidential election. With party leaders like Mario Cuomo and Dick Gephardt staying out of the running, the 1992 Democratic primary field consisted of relatively unknown candidates. Among those who sought the Democratic nomination were former senator Paul Tsongas of Massachusetts, former governor Jerry Brown of California, and Bill Clinton, who had served as the governor of Arkansas since 1983. Clinton emerged as the front-runner for the nomination after the first set of primaries in February 1992. A founding member of the centrist Democratic Leadership Council, Clinton overcame opposition from more liberal Democrats like Brown and clinched the Democratic nomination in April 1992.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Bill_Clinton#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilentz2008317%E2%80%93319-4)
Bush defeated a challenge from conservative commentator Pat Buchanan to win his party's nomination. Meanwhile, independent candidate Ross Perot, a billionaire businessman from Texas, emerged as a major factor in the race. Perot ran a populist campaign that focused on voters disillusioned with both parties, and he emphasized his opposition to the North American Free Trade Agreement and his desire to balance the federal budget. Polls taken in early June 1992 showed Bush leading the race, followed by Perot and then Clinton. From July to September, Perot temporarily dropped out of the race, causing severe damage to his candidacy. At the 1992 Democratic National Convention, Clinton selected Senator Al Gore of Tennessee as his running mate, and the successful convention helped unify Democrats behind Clinton. While the 1992 Republican National Convention placed a heavy emphasis on social issues, Clinton's campaign focused on the state of the economy, which was still emerging from the early 1990s recession.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Bill_Clinton#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilentz2008315%E2%80%93321-5)

William Jefferson Clinton (né Blythe III; born August 19, 1946) is an American retired politician and lawyer who served as the 42nd president of the United States from 1993 to 2001. A member of the Democratic Party, he previously served as the attorney general of Arkansas from 1977 to 1979, the governor of Arkansas from 1979 to 1981, and governor again from 1983 to 1992. His centrist Third Way political philosophy became known as Clintonism, which defined his presidency and the succeeding decades of the Democratic Party into the 21st century.

Born and raised in Arkansas, Clinton graduated from Georgetown University in 1968, and later from Yale Law School, where he met his future wife, Hillary Rodham. After graduating from law school, Clinton returned to Arkansas and won election as state attorney general, followed by two non-consecutive tenures as Arkansas governor. As governor, he overhauled the state's education system and served as chairman of the National Governors Association. Running as a "New Democrat", Clinton was elected president in the 1992 election, defeating the incumbent Republican president George H. W. Bush, and the independent businessman Ross Perot. He became the first president to be born in the Baby Boomer generation and the youngest to serve two full terms.
Clinton presided over the longest American period of peacetime economic expansion at the time. He signed into law the North American Free Trade Agreement, the Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act and the Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act. He failed, however, to pass his plan for national health care reform, and accepted a controversial compromise policy to his original plan to allow gay and lesbian service members to serve openly in the military. Starting in the mid-1990s, after Democrats were soundly defeated in the 1994 midterms, he began an ideological evolution as he became much more conservative in his domestic policy, advocating for and signing the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Act and Republican-led financial deregulation measures, while still championing liberal policy such as the State Children's Health Insurance Program. He appointed Ruth Bader Ginsburg and Stephen Breyer to the U.S. Supreme Court. In foreign policy, Clinton ordered U.S. military intervention in the Bosnian and Kosovo wars, eventually signing the Dayton Peace agreement. He also called for the expansion of NATO in Eastern Europe and many former Warsaw Pact members joined NATO during his presidency. Clinton's foreign policy in the Middle East saw him sign the Iraq Liberation Act which gave aid to groups against Saddam Hussein. He also participated in the Oslo I Accord and Camp David Summit to advance the Israeli–Palestinian peace process, and assisted the Northern Ireland peace process.

## Who Is Bill Clinton?
William Jefferson Clinton was the president of the United States from January 20, 1993, until January 20, 2001. He was the last person to serve as president during the 20th century and the first to serve during the 21st. Clinton was a Democrat who had previously served as the governor of the state of Arkansas. He served two full terms in office and was succeeded by George W. Bush.
Clinton's presidency was marked by some major changes in American politics, as well as several scandals.

# Bill Clinton | Biography, Presidency & Accomplishments
## Bill Clinton: Biography
**Bill Clinton** was born in a small town called Hope in the state of Arkansas on August 19, 1946. Clinton was the first baby boomer to ever become president. A baby boomer is a person who was born between 1946 and 1965. Clinton's name at birth was William Jefferson Blythe III. His biological father died when Bill was an infant, and Bill's mother, Virginia, married Roger Clinton in 1950. Roger and Virginia had a child, Roger Jr, who was Bill Clinton's only sibling. (Virginia Clinton died in 1994.)
Bill took his adopted father's last name when he was 15 years old.

# Bill Clinton | Biography, Presidency & Accomplishments
## Bill Clinton: Biography
### Early Years and Education
Bill Clinton and his mother were the victims of abuse at the hands of Roger Sr. In 1962, Roger and Virginia divorced. Virginia remarried Roger that same year and divorced him again in 1967. Despite Bill's tumultuous childhood, he was able to do very well at school. Clinton graduated from Hot Springs High School at the top of his class. In 1963, Clinton met President John F. Kennedy on a trip to Washington, DC as a member of Boys Nation (a youth political league.) He also met Arkansa's powerful senator, William Fulbright. Both Kennedy and Fulbright inspired Clinton to seek a career in politics.
Clinton earned a scholarship to study at Georgetown University in Washington, D.C. He earned a B.S. in Foreign Service in 1968. While at Georgetown, Clinton won a Rhodes Scholarship. A Rhodes Scholarship is a grant to study at Oxford University. It is considered to be one of the most prestigious scholarships in the world. After earning a second bachelor's at Oxford, Clinton entered Yale law school.

# Bill Clinton | Biography, Presidency & Accomplishments
## Bill Clinton: Biography
### Law School and the Start of Clinton's Political Career
Clinton met his wife, Hillary Rodham, while at Yale. After graduating, the couple moved back to Bill's home state where he began a career in politics. Hillary worked as a lawyer in Arkansas. In 1976, Bill Clinton was elected as Arkansas's attorney general. A state's attorney general is its chief law-enforcement official, and this position was a good stepping stone on the path to the White House.

# Bill Clinton | Biography, Presidency & Accomplishments
## Bill Clinton: Biography
### Governor of Arkansas
In 1976, Clinton was elected as Arkansas's governor. In that year, he ran against Lynne Lowe. Governor Bill Clinton served one term in that office before being defeated by Frank D. White in his reelection campaign. However, he ran a third time against White in 1982 and was subsequently reelected. Clinton remained the governor of Arkansas until December 12, 1992.
While governor, Clinton successfully worked to improve the state's roads and educational system. He also raised the state's taxes (something that was unpopular among many voters). During his time as governor, Clinton rose to become the chairman of the National Governors Association. His experience in this position was also seen as giving him useful experience in national politics.

# Bill Clinton | Biography, Presidency & Accomplishments
## Bill Clinton: Biography
### Bill Clinton's Presidency
Bill Clinton ran against George H.W. Bush during the 1992 presidential election. Bush had been the vice president of the United States for eight years during the Reagan administration and was himself elected president in 1988. A third-party candidate, Ross Perot, also ran that year. Clinton won the election with only 43.0% of the popular vote and 370 electoral votes. Many Republicans blamed Perot's candidacy for Bush's loss during the election.
Clinton entered the presidency with a Democratic majority in both houses of Congress. This gave him the ability to pass some major pieces of legislation. Here is a list of some of the major issues and accomplishments that marked the first term of the Clinton presidency:
*   Healthcare Reform - Healthcare reform was a major issue during the presidential campaign. Clinton assigned First Lady Hillary Clinton the task of reforming America's healthcare system. However, she was not able to come up with a plan that could pass Congress. This failure was seen as a major setback for the Clinton presidency.  
*   Gay men and lesbians in the military - Allowing gay men and lesbians to serve openly in the military was another campaign promise made by Clinton. However, there was a great deal of resistance to this from both Republicans and Democrats. The so-called "Don't ask, don't tell" policy was adopted as a compromise. This would allow gay men and lesbians to serve in the military, as long as they kept their sexual orientation a secret.  
*   Gun Control - Clinton signed the Brady Bill into law. This law was a comprehensive piece of gun-control legislation that was extremely unpopular among conservatives.  
*   Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act of 1994 - This law reformed law enforcement in the United States and lead to a higher rate of incarceration nationwide. This law had supporters and detractors on both sides of the political aisle.
In 1994, Clinton's unpopularity lead to the Republican takeover of both the House and the Senate. However, many commentators believed that this fact actually helped Clinton to win reelection in 1996. The Republican Congress proved to be unpopular among many swing voters. As a result, Clinton beat Bob Dole during the presidential election of 1996 and received a popular vote of 49.2%.

# Bill Clinton | Biography, Presidency & Accomplishments
## Bill Clinton: Biography
### Bill Clinton's Presidency
Clinton's second term was marked by major conflicts with Congress. Despite losing seats, the Republicans managed to remain in control of both houses of Congress for the remainder of the Clinton presidency. The combative nature between Clinton and Congress came to a head when the House of Representatives impeached Clinton in 1998. Clinton lied while under oath about having an affair with **Monica Lewinsky**, a former White House Intern. Since lying under oath is a crime, Republicans felt that they had the duty to impeach the president.
In 1998, Clinton became the second president in U.S. history to be impeached; however, he was found not guilty by the Senate and continued to serve the remainder of his term. The majority of Americans, including many who did not support Clinton, felt that the impeachment was a political witch hunt.
Clinton left office in 2001 with very high approval ratings.

# Bill Clinton | Biography, Presidency & Accomplishments
## Early Life & Education
Clinton graduated high school in 1964 and enrolled at Georgetown University. Graduating from the university in 1968, he earned a prestigious Rhodes Scholarship to Oxford University in England. Upon his arrival in England, he received his Draft Notice, forcing him to return to Arkansas. He avoided being drafted, though, by stating he would enroll in both the University of Arkansas School of Law and ROTC. Instead, however, he went back to Oxford and, feeling somewhat guilty about his attempt to avoid the draft, he resubmitted his name to the Draft Board. A lottery system was in effect, and Clinton's number was so high he was assured of not being sent to Vietnam, where the war had been active for some time.
After Oxford, Clinton returned to the United States and enrolled at Yale University to complete his law studies. While there, he met **Hillary Rodham** and both of them graduated in 1973. By 1975, they were married and returned to Arkansas.

# Bill Clinton | Biography, Presidency & Accomplishments
## Accomplishments as Governor & President
Settling in Fayetteville, Arkansas, Bill Clinton began teaching at the University of Arkansas Law School. In 1974, he ran an unsuccessful campaign against Republican Congressman Paul Hammerschmidt, who represented Arkansas in the House of Representatives. However, the process made him a rising star in the Arkansas political pool, and he won the election as the state **Attorney General** in 1976.
In 1978, Clinton easily defeated Republican Lynn Lowe, claiming Arkansas governorship at the age of 32--one of the youngest state governors in US history. In his first term, he sought to reform the state's health and educational services. However, he made mistakes when he hiked the auto registration tax and roughly handled a Cuban refugee policy at nearby Ft. Chaffee.
In 1980, an obscure Republican challenger, Frank White, defeated Clinton. In 1982, he admitted his mistakes and was elected once again as Governor of Arkansas. Through 1986-87, he was Chairman of the National Governors Association and served on the Democratic Leadership Council.
In 1992, the Democratic Party chose Bill Clinton as their **candidate for president**, and he ultimately defeated George H.W. Bush on November 3rd, 1992, becoming the **42nd President of the United States**. He assumed the position in January of 1993.
One of his first-term notable accomplishments included the passage of NAFTA, the North American Free Trade Agreement, which ended import duties between the United States, Canada, and Mexico. With Hillary, Bill sought to get a Health Plan through Congress, but it was ultimately futile.
Bill Clinton won a 2nd term in 1996, defeating Republican Senator **Bob Dole**, of Kansas. By far, the greatest accomplishment of his second term was his role in the economic boost. More Americans owned homes, inflation was low, and there was even a budget surplus amounting to over 500 million dollars.

# Bill Clinton | Biography, Presidency & Accomplishments
## Accomplishments as Governor & President
However, his 2nd term and presidency were marred by an affair with a White House Intern, named **Monica Lewinsky**. This resulted in President Clinton becoming the 2nd president to be impeached by Congress. There were enough votes to convict the president in the House of Representatives, but not in the Senate where a two-thirds vote was needed (he was retained by one vote). Clinton's 2nd term ended in 2001, following the historic 2000 election where Texas Governor, George W. Bush, prevailed to become the next president.

# Bill Clinton | Biography, Presidency & Accomplishments
## Lesson Summary
We have seen how William Jefferson Clinton, more commonly referred to as Bill Clinton, overcame an abusive stepfather and poverty to attend one of the nation's most prestigious universities, where he would rise to become a lawyer. From his teaching post at the University of Arkansas Law School, he launched a political career that began as Attorney General, then Governor of Arkansas. From there he was elected to two terms as US President, starting in 1993.

## Who Is Bill Clinton?
William Jefferson Clinton was the president of the United States from January 20, 1993, until January 20, 2001. He was the last person to serve as president during the 20th century and the first to serve during the 21st. Clinton was a Democrat who had previously served as the governor of the state of Arkansas. He served two full terms in office and was succeeded by George W. Bush.
Clinton's presidency was marked by some major changes in American politics, as well as several scandals.

# Bill Clinton | Biography, Presidency & Accomplishments
## Bill Clinton: Biography
**Bill Clinton** was born in a small town called Hope in the state of Arkansas on August 19, 1946. Clinton was the first baby boomer to ever become president. A baby boomer is a person who was born between 1946 and 1965. Clinton's name at birth was William Jefferson Blythe III. His biological father died when Bill was an infant, and Bill's mother, Virginia, married Roger Clinton in 1950. Roger and Virginia had a child, Roger Jr, who was Bill Clinton's only sibling. (Virginia Clinton died in 1994.)
Bill took his adopted father's last name when he was 15 years old.

# Bill Clinton | Biography, Presidency & Accomplishments
## Bill Clinton: Biography
### Early Years and Education
Bill Clinton and his mother were the victims of abuse at the hands of Roger Sr. In 1962, Roger and Virginia divorced. Virginia remarried Roger that same year and divorced him again in 1967. Despite Bill's tumultuous childhood, he was able to do very well at school. Clinton graduated from Hot Springs High School at the top of his class. In 1963, Clinton met President John F. Kennedy on a trip to Washington, DC as a member of Boys Nation (a youth political league.) He also met Arkansa's powerful senator, William Fulbright. Both Kennedy and Fulbright inspired Clinton to seek a career in politics.
Clinton earned a scholarship to study at Georgetown University in Washington, D.C. He earned a B.S. in Foreign Service in 1968. While at Georgetown, Clinton won a Rhodes Scholarship. A Rhodes Scholarship is a grant to study at Oxford University. It is considered to be one of the most prestigious scholarships in the world. After earning a second bachelor's at Oxford, Clinton entered Yale law school.

## Bill Clinton: Biography
### Law School and the Start of Clinton's Political Career
Clinton met his wife, Hillary Rodham, while at Yale. After graduating, the couple moved back to Bill's home state where he began a career in politics. Hillary worked as a lawyer in Arkansas. In 1976, Bill Clinton was elected as Arkansas's attorney general. A state's attorney general is its chief law-enforcement official, and this position was a good stepping stone on the path to the White House.

# Bill Clinton | Biography, Presidency & Accomplishments
## Bill Clinton: Biography
### Governor of Arkansas
In 1976, Clinton was elected as Arkansas's governor. In that year, he ran against Lynne Lowe. Governor Bill Clinton served one term in that office before being defeated by Frank D. White in his reelection campaign. However, he ran a third time against White in 1982 and was subsequently reelected. Clinton remained the governor of Arkansas until December 12, 1992.
While governor, Clinton successfully worked to improve the state's roads and educational system. He also raised the state's taxes (something that was unpopular among many voters). During his time as governor, Clinton rose to become the chairman of the National Governors Association. His experience in this position was also seen as giving him useful experience in national politics.

# Bill Clinton | Biography, Presidency & Accomplishments
## Bill Clinton: Biography
### Bill Clinton's Presidency
Bill Clinton ran against George H.W. Bush during the 1992 presidential election. Bush had been the vice president of the United States for eight years during the Reagan administration and was himself elected president in 1988. A third-party candidate, Ross Perot, also ran that year. Clinton won the election with only 43.0% of the popular vote and 370 electoral votes. Many Republicans blamed Perot's candidacy for Bush's loss during the election.
Clinton entered the presidency with a Democratic majority in both houses of Congress. This gave him the ability to pass some major pieces of legislation. Here is a list of some of the major issues and accomplishments that marked the first term of the Clinton presidency:
*   Healthcare Reform - Healthcare reform was a major issue during the presidential campaign. Clinton assigned First Lady Hillary Clinton the task of reforming America's healthcare system. However, she was not able to come up with a plan that could pass Congress. This failure was seen as a major setback for the Clinton presidency.  
*   Gay men and lesbians in the military - Allowing gay men and lesbians to serve openly in the military was another campaign promise made by Clinton. However, there was a great deal of resistance to this from both Republicans and Democrats. The so-called "Don't ask, don't tell" policy was adopted as a compromise. This would allow gay men and lesbians to serve in the military, as long as they kept their sexual orientation a secret.  
*   Gun Control - Clinton signed the Brady Bill into law. This law was a comprehensive piece of gun-control legislation that was extremely unpopular among conservatives.  
*   Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act of 1994 - This law reformed law enforcement in the United States and lead to a higher rate of incarceration nationwide. This law had supporters and detractors on both sides of the political aisle.
In 1994, Clinton's unpopularity lead to the Republican takeover of both the House and the Senate. However, many commentators believed that this fact actually helped Clinton to win reelection in 1996. The Republican Congress proved to be unpopular among many swing voters. As a result, Clinton beat Bob Dole during the presidential election of 1996 and received a popular vote of 49.2%.

# Bill Clinton | Biography, Presidency & Accomplishments
## Bill Clinton: Biography
### Bill Clinton's Presidency
Clinton's second term was marked by major conflicts with Congress. Despite losing seats, the Republicans managed to remain in control of both houses of Congress for the remainder of the Clinton presidency. The combative nature between Clinton and Congress came to a head when the House of Representatives impeached Clinton in 1998. Clinton lied while under oath about having an affair with **Monica Lewinsky**, a former White House Intern. Since lying under oath is a crime, Republicans felt that they had the duty to impeach the president.
In 1998, Clinton became the second president in U.S. history to be impeached; however, he was found not guilty by the Senate and continued to serve the remainder of his term. The majority of Americans, including many who did not support Clinton, felt that the impeachment was a political witch hunt.
Clinton left office in 2001 with very high approval ratings.

# Bill Clinton | Biography, Presidency & Accomplishments
## Early Life & Education
Clinton graduated high school in 1964 and enrolled at Georgetown University. Graduating from the university in 1968, he earned a prestigious Rhodes Scholarship to Oxford University in England. Upon his arrival in England, he received his Draft Notice, forcing him to return to Arkansas. He avoided being drafted, though, by stating he would enroll in both the University of Arkansas School of Law and ROTC. Instead, however, he went back to Oxford and, feeling somewhat guilty about his attempt to avoid the draft, he resubmitted his name to the Draft Board. A lottery system was in effect, and Clinton's number was so high he was assured of not being sent to Vietnam, where the war had been active for some time.
After Oxford, Clinton returned to the United States and enrolled at Yale University to complete his law studies. While there, he met **Hillary Rodham** and both of them graduated in 1973. By 1975, they were married and returned to Arkansas.

# Bill Clinton | Biography, Presidency & Accomplishments
## Accomplishments as Governor & President
Settling in Fayetteville, Arkansas, Bill Clinton began teaching at the University of Arkansas Law School. In 1974, he ran an unsuccessful campaign against Republican Congressman Paul Hammerschmidt, who represented Arkansas in the House of Representatives. However, the process made him a rising star in the Arkansas political pool, and he won the election as the state **Attorney General** in 1976.
In 1978, Clinton easily defeated Republican Lynn Lowe, claiming Arkansas governorship at the age of 32--one of the youngest state governors in US history. In his first term, he sought to reform the state's health and educational services. However, he made mistakes when he hiked the auto registration tax and roughly handled a Cuban refugee policy at nearby Ft. Chaffee.
In 1980, an obscure Republican challenger, Frank White, defeated Clinton. In 1982, he admitted his mistakes and was elected once again as Governor of Arkansas. Through 1986-87, he was Chairman of the National Governors Association and served on the Democratic Leadership Council.
In 1992, the Democratic Party chose Bill Clinton as their **candidate for president**, and he ultimately defeated George H.W. Bush on November 3rd, 1992, becoming the **42nd President of the United States**. He assumed the position in January of 1993.
One of his first-term notable accomplishments included the passage of NAFTA, the North American Free Trade Agreement, which ended import duties between the United States, Canada, and Mexico. With Hillary, Bill sought to get a Health Plan through Congress, but it was ultimately futile.
Bill Clinton won a 2nd term in 1996, defeating Republican Senator **Bob Dole**, of Kansas. By far, the greatest accomplishment of his second term was his role in the economic boost. More Americans owned homes, inflation was low, and there was even a budget surplus amounting to over 500 million dollars.

# Bill Clinton | Biography, Presidency & Accomplishments
## Accomplishments as Governor & President
However, his 2nd term and presidency were marred by an affair with a White House Intern, named **Monica Lewinsky**. This resulted in President Clinton becoming the 2nd president to be impeached by Congress. There were enough votes to convict the president in the House of Representatives, but not in the Senate where a two-thirds vote was needed (he was retained by one vote). Clinton's 2nd term ended in 2001, following the historic 2000 election where Texas Governor, George W. Bush, prevailed to become the next president.

Bill Clinton's tenure as the 42nd president of the United States began with his first inauguration on January 20, 1993, and ended on January 20, 2001. Clinton, a Democrat from Arkansas, took office after defeating the Republican incumbent president George H. W. Bush and independent businessman Ross Perot in the 1992 presidential election. Four years later, he won re-election in the 1996 presidential election, after defeating the Republican nominee Bob Dole, and also Perot again (then as the nominee of the Reform Party). Alongside Clinton's presidency, the Democratic Party also held their majorities in the House of Representatives and the Senate during the 103rd U.S. Congress following the 1992 elections, thereby attained an overall federal government trifecta. Clinton was constitutionally limited to two terms (the first re-elected Democrat president to be so) and was succeeded by Republican George W. Bush, who won the 2000 presidential election against Clinton'ds preferred successor, Vice President Al Gore.
texts.1: President Clinton oversaw the second longest period of peacetime economic expansion[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Bill_Clinton#cite_note-1) in American history. Months into his first term, he signed the Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1993, which raised taxes and set the stage for future budget surpluses. He signed the bipartisan Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act and won ratification of the North American Free Trade Agreement, despite opposition from trade unions and environmentalists. Clinton's most ambitious legislative initiative, a plan to provide universal health care, failed to advance through Congress. A backlash to Clinton's agenda sparked the Republican Revolution, with the GOP taking control of the House of Representatives for the first time in 40 years. Clinton pivoted to the center in response by assembling a bipartisan coalition to pass welfare reform, and he successfully expanded [health insurance for children](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Children's_Health_Insurance_Program "State Children's Health Insurance Program").
texts.2:
While Clinton's economy was strong, his presidency oscillated dramatically from high to low and back again, which historian Gil Troy characterized in six Acts. Act I in early 1993 was "Bush League" with amateurish distractions. By mid-1993 Clinton had recovered to Act II, passing a balanced budget and the NAFTA trade deal. Act III, 1994, saw the Republicans mobilizing under Newt Gingrich, defeating Clinton's healthcare reforms, and taking control of the House of Representatives for the first time in forty years. The years 1995 to 1997 saw the comeback in Act IV, with a triumphant reelection landslide in 1996. However, Act V, the Clinton–Lewinsky scandal and impeachment made 1998 a lost year. Clinton concluded happily with Act VI by deregulating the banking system in 1999.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Bill_Clinton#cite_note-2) In foreign policy, Clinton initiated a bombing campaign in the Balkans, which led to the creation of a United Nations protectorate in Kosovo. He played a major role of the expansion of NATO into former Eastern Bloc countries and remained on positive terms with Russian presidentBoris Yeltsin. During his second term, Clinton presided over the deregulation of the financial and telecommunications industry. Clinton's second term also saw the first federal budget surpluses since the 1960s. The ratio of debt held by the public to GDP fell from 47.8% in 1993 to 33.6% by 2000. His impeachment in 1998 arose after he denied claims of having an affair with a White House intern, Monica Lewinsky under oath. He was acquitted of all charges by the Senate. He appointed Ruth Bader Ginsburg and Stephen Breyer to the U.S. Supreme Court.
With a 66% approval rating at the time he left office, Clinton had the highest exit approval rating of any president since the end of World War II.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Bill_Clinton#cite_note-3) Despite the Clinton–Lewinsky scandal and numerous high-profile controversies, historians and political scientists generally rank Clinton as an above-average president.

Incumbent president George H. W. Bush and President-elect Clinton on November 18, 1992.
President George H. W. Bush's popularity in the aftermath of the successful 1991 Gulf War convinced many prominent Democrats to sit out the 1992 presidential election. With party leaders like Mario Cuomo and Dick Gephardt staying out of the running, the 1992 Democratic primary field consisted of relatively unknown candidates. Among those who sought the Democratic nomination were former senator Paul Tsongas of Massachusetts, former governor Jerry Brown of California, and Bill Clinton, who had served as the governor of Arkansas since 1983. Clinton emerged as the front-runner for the nomination after the first set of primaries in February 1992. A founding member of the centrist Democratic Leadership Council, Clinton overcame opposition from more liberal Democrats like Brown and clinched the Democratic nomination in April 1992.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Bill_Clinton#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilentz2008317%E2%80%93319-4)
Bush defeated a challenge from conservative commentator Pat Buchanan to win his party's nomination. Meanwhile, independent candidate Ross Perot, a billionaire businessman from Texas, emerged as a major factor in the race. Perot ran a populist campaign that focused on voters disillusioned with both parties, and he emphasized his opposition to the North American Free Trade Agreement and his desire to balance the federal budget. Polls taken in early June 1992 showed Bush leading the race, followed by Perot and then Clinton. From July to September, Perot temporarily dropped out of the race, causing severe damage to his candidacy. At the 1992 Democratic National Convention, Clinton selected Senator Al Gore of Tennessee as his running mate, and the successful convention helped unify Democrats behind Clinton. While the 1992 Republican National Convention placed a heavy emphasis on social issues, Clinton's campaign focused on the state of the economy, which was still emerging from the early 1990s recession.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Bill_Clinton#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilentz2008315%E2%80%93321-5)

William Jefferson Clinton (né Blythe III; born August 19, 1946) is an American retired politician and lawyer who served as the 42nd president of the United States from 1993 to 2001. A member of the Democratic Party, he previously served as the attorney general of Arkansas from 1977 to 1979, the governor of Arkansas from 1979 to 1981, and governor again from 1983 to 1992. His centrist Third Way political philosophy became known as Clintonism, which defined his presidency and the succeeding decades of the Democratic Party into the 21st century.
texts.2:
Born and raised in Arkansas, Clinton graduated from Georgetown University in 1968, and later from Yale Law School, where he met his future wife, Hillary Rodham. After graduating from law school, Clinton returned to Arkansas and won election as state attorney general, followed by two non-consecutive tenures as Arkansas governor. As governor, he overhauled the state's education system and served as chairman of the National Governors Association. Running as a "New Democrat", Clinton was elected president in the 1992 election, defeating the incumbent Republican president George H. W. Bush, and the independent businessman Ross Perot. He became the first president to be born in the Baby Boomer generation and the youngest to serve two full terms.
Clinton presided over the longest American period of peacetime economic expansion at the time. He signed into law the North American Free Trade Agreement, the Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act and the Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act. He failed, however, to pass his plan for national health care reform, and accepted a controversial compromise policy to his original plan to allow gay and lesbian service members to serve openly in the military. Starting in the mid-1990s, after Democrats were soundly defeated in the 1994 midterms, he began an ideological evolution as he became much more conservative in his domestic policy, advocating for and signing the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Act and Republican-led financial deregulation measures, while still championing liberal policy such as the State Children's Health Insurance Program. He appointed Ruth Bader Ginsburg and Stephen Breyer to the U.S. Supreme Court. In foreign policy, Clinton ordered U.S. military intervention in the Bosnian and Kosovo wars, eventually signing the Dayton Peace agreement. He also called for the expansion of NATO in Eastern Europe and many former Warsaw Pact members joined NATO during his presidency. Clinton's foreign policy in the Middle East saw him sign the Iraq Liberation Act which gave aid to groups against Saddam Hussein. He also participated in the Oslo I Accord and Camp David Summit to advance the Israeli–Palestinian peace process, and assisted the Northern Ireland peace process.

# Bill Clinton | Biography, Presidency & Accomplishments
## Bill Clinton: Biography
**Bill Clinton** was born in a small town called Hope in the state of Arkansas on August 19, 1946. Clinton was the first baby boomer to ever become president. A baby boomer is a person who was born between 1946 and 1965. Clinton's name at birth was William Jefferson Blythe III. His biological father died when Bill was an infant, and Bill's mother, Virginia, married Roger Clinton in 1950. Roger and Virginia had a child, Roger Jr, who was Bill Clinton's only sibling. (Virginia Clinton died in 1994.)
Bill took his adopted father's last name when he was 15 years old.

# Bill Clinton | Biography, Presidency & Accomplishments
## Bill Clinton: Biography
### Early Years and Education
Bill Clinton and his mother were the victims of abuse at the hands of Roger Sr. In 1962, Roger and Virginia divorced. Virginia remarried Roger that same year and divorced him again in 1967. Despite Bill's tumultuous childhood, he was able to do very well at school. Clinton graduated from Hot Springs High School at the top of his class. In 1963, Clinton met President John F. Kennedy on a trip to Washington, DC as a member of Boys Nation (a youth political league.) He also met Arkansa's powerful senator, William Fulbright. Both Kennedy and Fulbright inspired Clinton to seek a career in politics.
Clinton earned a scholarship to study at Georgetown University in Washington, D.C. He earned a B.S. in Foreign Service in 1968. While at Georgetown, Clinton won a Rhodes Scholarship. A Rhodes Scholarship is a grant to study at Oxford University. It is considered to be one of the most prestigious scholarships in the world. After earning a second bachelor's at Oxford, Clinton entered Yale law school.

# Bill Clinton | Biography, Presidency & Accomplishments
## Bill Clinton: Biography
### Law School and the Start of Clinton's Political Career
Clinton met his wife, Hillary Rodham, while at Yale. After graduating, the couple moved back to Bill's home state where he began a career in politics. Hillary worked as a lawyer in Arkansas. In 1976, Bill Clinton was elected as Arkansas's attorney general. A state's attorney general is its chief law-enforcement official, and this position was a good stepping stone on the path to the White House.

# Bill Clinton | Biography, Presidency & Accomplishments
## Bill Clinton: Biography
### Governor of Arkansas
In 1976, Clinton was elected as Arkansas's governor. In that year, he ran against Lynne Lowe. Governor Bill Clinton served one term in that office before being defeated by Frank D. White in his reelection campaign. However, he ran a third time against White in 1982 and was subsequently reelected. Clinton remained the governor of Arkansas until December 12, 1992.
While governor, Clinton successfully worked to improve the state's roads and educational system. He also raised the state's taxes (something that was unpopular among many voters). During his time as governor, Clinton rose to become the chairman of the National Governors Association. His experience in this position was also seen as giving him useful experience in national politics.

# Bill Clinton | Biography, Presidency & Accomplishments
## Bill Clinton: Biography
### Bill Clinton's Presidency
Bill Clinton ran against George H.W. Bush during the 1992 presidential election. Bush had been the vice president of the United States for eight years during the Reagan administration and was himself elected president in 1988. A third-party candidate, Ross Perot, also ran that year. Clinton won the election with only 43.0% of the popular vote and 370 electoral votes. Many Republicans blamed Perot's candidacy for Bush's loss during the election.
Clinton entered the presidency with a Democratic majority in both houses of Congress. This gave him the ability to pass some major pieces of legislation. Here is a list of some of the major issues and accomplishments that marked the first term of the Clinton presidency:
*   Healthcare Reform - Healthcare reform was a major issue during the presidential campaign. Clinton assigned First Lady Hillary Clinton the task of reforming America's healthcare system. However, she was not able to come up with a plan that could pass Congress. This failure was seen as a major setback for the Clinton presidency.  
*   Gay men and lesbians in the military - Allowing gay men and lesbians to serve openly in the military was another campaign promise made by Clinton. However, there was a great deal of resistance to this from both Republicans and Democrats. The so-called "Don't ask, don't tell" policy was adopted as a compromise. This would allow gay men and lesbians to serve in the military, as long as they kept their sexual orientation a secret.  
*   Gun Control - Clinton signed the Brady Bill into law. This law was a comprehensive piece of gun-control legislation that was extremely unpopular among conservatives.  
*   Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act of 1994 - This law reformed law enforcement in the United States and lead to a higher rate of incarceration nationwide. This law had supporters and detractors on both sides of the political aisle.
In 1994, Clinton's unpopularity lead to the Republican takeover of both the House and the Senate. However, many commentators believed that this fact actually helped Clinton to win reelection in 1996. The Republican Congress proved to be unpopular among many swing voters. As a result, Clinton beat Bob Dole during the presidential election of 1996 and received a popular vote of 49.2%.

## Bill Clinton: Biography
### Bill Clinton's Presidency
Clinton's second term was marked by major conflicts with Congress. Despite losing seats, the Republicans managed to remain in control of both houses of Congress for the remainder of the Clinton presidency. The combative nature between Clinton and Congress came to a head when the House of Representatives impeached Clinton in 1998. Clinton lied while under oath about having an affair with **Monica Lewinsky**, a former White House Intern. Since lying under oath is a crime, Republicans felt that they had the duty to impeach the president.
In 1998, Clinton became the second president in U.S. history to be impeached; however, he was found not guilty by the Senate and continued to serve the remainder of his term. The majority of Americans, including many who did not support Clinton, felt that the impeachment was a political witch hunt.
Clinton left office in 2001 with very high approval ratings.

# Bill Clinton | Biography, Presidency & Accomplishments
## Early Life & Education
Clinton graduated high school in 1964 and enrolled at Georgetown University. Graduating from the university in 1968, he earned a prestigious Rhodes Scholarship to Oxford University in England. Upon his arrival in England, he received his Draft Notice, forcing him to return to Arkansas. He avoided being drafted, though, by stating he would enroll in both the University of Arkansas School of Law and ROTC. Instead, however, he went back to Oxford and, feeling somewhat guilty about his attempt to avoid the draft, he resubmitted his name to the Draft Board. A lottery system was in effect, and Clinton's number was so high he was assured of not being sent to Vietnam, where the war had been active for some time.
After Oxford, Clinton returned to the United States and enrolled at Yale University to complete his law studies. While there, he met **Hillary Rodham** and both of them graduated in 1973. By 1975, they were married and returned to Arkansas.

# Bill Clinton | Biography, Presidency & Accomplishments
## Accomplishments as Governor & President
Settling in Fayetteville, Arkansas, Bill Clinton began teaching at the University of Arkansas Law School. In 1974, he ran an unsuccessful campaign against Republican Congressman Paul Hammerschmidt, who represented Arkansas in the House of Representatives. However, the process made him a rising star in the Arkansas political pool, and he won the election as the state **Attorney General** in 1976.
In 1978, Clinton easily defeated Republican Lynn Lowe, claiming Arkansas governorship at the age of 32--one of the youngest state governors in US history. In his first term, he sought to reform the state's health and educational services. However, he made mistakes when he hiked the auto registration tax and roughly handled a Cuban refugee policy at nearby Ft. Chaffee.
In 1980, an obscure Republican challenger, Frank White, defeated Clinton. In 1982, he admitted his mistakes and was elected once again as Governor of Arkansas. Through 1986-87, he was Chairman of the National Governors Association and served on the Democratic Leadership Council.
In 1992, the Democratic Party chose Bill Clinton as their **candidate for president**, and he ultimately defeated George H.W. Bush on November 3rd, 1992, becoming the **42nd President of the United States**. He assumed the position in January of 1993.
One of his first-term notable accomplishments included the passage of NAFTA, the North American Free Trade Agreement, which ended import duties between the United States, Canada, and Mexico. With Hillary, Bill sought to get a Health Plan through Congress, but it was ultimately futile.
Bill Clinton won a 2nd term in 1996, defeating Republican Senator **Bob Dole**, of Kansas. By far, the greatest accomplishment of his second term was his role in the economic boost. More Americans owned homes, inflation was low, and there was even a budget surplus amounting to over 500 million dollars.

# Bill Clinton | Biography, Presidency & Accomplishments
## Accomplishments as Governor & President
However, his 2nd term and presidency were marred by an affair with a White House Intern, named **Monica Lewinsky**. This resulted in President Clinton becoming the 2nd president to be impeached by Congress. There were enough votes to convict the president in the House of Representatives, but not in the Senate where a two-thirds vote was needed (he was retained by one vote). Clinton's 2nd term ended in 2001, following the historic 2000 election where Texas Governor, George W. Bush, prevailed to become the next president.

Bill Clinton's tenure as the 42nd president of the United States began with his first inauguration on January 20, 1993, and ended on January 20, 2001. Clinton, a Democrat from Arkansas, took office after defeating the Republican incumbent president George H. W. Bush and independent businessman Ross Perot in the 1992 presidential election. Four years later, he won re-election in the 1996 presidential election, after defeating the Republican nominee Bob Dole, and also Perot again (then as the nominee of the Reform Party). Alongside Clinton's presidency, the Democratic Party also held their majorities in the House of Representatives and the Senate during the 103rd U.S. Congress following the 1992 elections, thereby attained an overall federal government trifecta. Clinton was constitutionally limited to two terms (the first re-elected Democrat president to be so) and was succeeded by Republican George W. Bush, who won the 2000 presidential election against Clinton'ds preferred successor, Vice President Al Gore.

President Clinton oversaw the second longest period of peacetime economic expansion[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Bill_Clinton#cite_note-1) in American history. Months into his first term, he signed the Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1993, which raised taxes and set the stage for future budget surpluses. He signed the bipartisan Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act and won ratification of the North American Free Trade Agreement, despite opposition from trade unions and environmentalists. Clinton's most ambitious legislative initiative, a plan to provide universal health care, failed to advance through Congress. A backlash to Clinton's agenda sparked the Republican Revolution, with the GOP taking control of the House of Representatives for the first time in 40 years. Clinton pivoted to the center in response by assembling a bipartisan coalition to pass welfare reform, and he successfully expanded [health insurance for children](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Children's_Health_Insurance_Program "State Children's Health Insurance Program").

While Clinton's economy was strong, his presidency oscillated dramatically from high to low and back again, which historian Gil Troy characterized in six Acts. Act I in early 1993 was "Bush League" with amateurish distractions. By mid-1993 Clinton had recovered to Act II, passing a balanced budget and the NAFTA trade deal. Act III, 1994, saw the Republicans mobilizing under Newt Gingrich, defeating Clinton's healthcare reforms, and taking control of the House of Representatives for the first time in forty years. The years 1995 to 1997 saw the comeback in Act IV, with a triumphant reelection landslide in 1996. However, Act V, the Clinton–Lewinsky scandal and impeachment made 1998 a lost year. Clinton concluded happily with Act VI by deregulating the banking system in 1999.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Bill_Clinton#cite_note-2) In foreign policy, Clinton initiated a bombing campaign in the Balkans, which led to the creation of a United Nations protectorate in Kosovo. He played a major role of the expansion of NATO into former Eastern Bloc countries and remained on positive terms with Russian presidentBoris Yeltsin. During his second term, Clinton presided over the deregulation of the financial and telecommunications industry. Clinton's second term also saw the first federal budget surpluses since the 1960s. The ratio of debt held by the public to GDP fell from 47.8% in 1993 to 33.6% by 2000. His impeachment in 1998 arose after he denied claims of having an affair with a White House intern, Monica Lewinsky under oath. He was acquitted of all charges by the Senate. He appointed Ruth Bader Ginsburg and Stephen Breyer to the U.S. Supreme Court.
With a 66% approval rating at the time he left office, Clinton had the highest exit approval rating of any president since the end of World War II.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Bill_Clinton#cite_note-3) Despite the Clinton–Lewinsky scandal and numerous high-profile controversies, historians and political scientists generally rank Clinton as an above-average president.
1992 Electoral College vote results

Incumbent president George H. W. Bush and President-elect Clinton on November 18, 1992.
President George H. W. Bush's popularity in the aftermath of the successful 1991 Gulf War convinced many prominent Democrats to sit out the 1992 presidential election. With party leaders like Mario Cuomo and Dick Gephardt staying out of the running, the 1992 Democratic primary field consisted of relatively unknown candidates. Among those who sought the Democratic nomination were former senator Paul Tsongas of Massachusetts, former governor Jerry Brown of California, and Bill Clinton, who had served as the governor of Arkansas since 1983. Clinton emerged as the front-runner for the nomination after the first set of primaries in February 1992. A founding member of the centrist Democratic Leadership Council, Clinton overcame opposition from more liberal Democrats like Brown and clinched the Democratic nomination in April 1992.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Bill_Clinton#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilentz2008317%E2%80%93319-4)
Bush defeated a challenge from conservative commentator Pat Buchanan to win his party's nomination. Meanwhile, independent candidate Ross Perot, a billionaire businessman from Texas, emerged as a major factor in the race. Perot ran a populist campaign that focused on voters disillusioned with both parties, and he emphasized his opposition to the North American Free Trade Agreement and his desire to balance the federal budget. Polls taken in early June 1992 showed Bush leading the race, followed by Perot and then Clinton. From July to September, Perot temporarily dropped out of the race, causing severe damage to his candidacy. At the 1992 Democratic National Convention, Clinton selected Senator Al Gore of Tennessee as his running mate, and the successful convention helped unify Democrats behind Clinton. While the 1992 Republican National Convention placed a heavy emphasis on social issues, Clinton's campaign focused on the state of the economy, which was still emerging from the early 1990s recession.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Bill_Clinton#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilentz2008315%E2%80%93321-5)

William Jefferson Clinton (né Blythe III; born August 19, 1946) is an American retired politician and lawyer who served as the 42nd president of the United States from 1993 to 2001. A member of the Democratic Party, he previously served as the attorney general of Arkansas from 1977 to 1979, the governor of Arkansas from 1979 to 1981, and governor again from 1983 to 1992. His centrist Third Way political philosophy became known as Clintonism, which defined his presidency and the succeeding decades of the Democratic Party into the 21st century.

Born and raised in Arkansas, Clinton graduated from Georgetown University in 1968, and later from Yale Law School, where he met his future wife, Hillary Rodham. After graduating from law school, Clinton returned to Arkansas and won election as state attorney general, followed by two non-consecutive tenures as Arkansas governor. As governor, he overhauled the state's education system and served as chairman of the National Governors Association. Running as a "New Democrat", Clinton was elected president in the 1992 election, defeating the incumbent Republican president George H. W. Bush, and the independent businessman Ross Perot. He became the first president to be born in the Baby Boomer generation and the youngest to serve two full terms.
Clinton presided over the longest American period of peacetime economic expansion at the time. He signed into law the North American Free Trade Agreement, the Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act and the Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act. He failed, however, to pass his plan for national health care reform, and accepted a controversial compromise policy to his original plan to allow gay and lesbian service members to serve openly in the military. Starting in the mid-1990s, after Democrats were soundly defeated in the 1994 midterms, he began an ideological evolution as he became much more conservative in his domestic policy, advocating for and signing the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Act and Republican-led financial deregulation measures, while still championing liberal policy such as the State Children's Health Insurance Program. He appointed Ruth Bader Ginsburg and Stephen Breyer to the U.S. Supreme Court. In foreign policy, Clinton ordered U.S. military intervention in the Bosnian and Kosovo wars, eventually signing the Dayton Peace agreement. He also called for the expansion of NATO in Eastern Europe and many former Warsaw Pact members joined NATO during his presidency. Clinton's foreign policy in the Middle East saw him sign the Iraq Liberation Act which gave aid to groups against Saddam Hussein. He also participated in the Oslo I Accord and Camp David Summit to advance the Israeli–Palestinian peace process, and assisted the Northern Ireland peace process.

Gymnastics events have been staged at the Olympic Games since 1896,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_female_artistic_gymnasts_for_the_United_States#cite_note-1) but women's events first appeared in 1928. American female gymnasts have participated in every Olympic Games since 1936, except for 1980.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_female_artistic_gymnasts_for_the_United_States#cite_note-team-2) A total of 90 female gymnasts have represented the United States. American women have won 62 medals at the Olympics – 11 in team all-around, 11 in individual all-around, 7 in vault, 10 in uneven bars, 11 in balance beam, and 12 in floor exercise. The medals include 19 golds. The U.S. has medaled in the team all-around in every Summer Olympics since 1992, winning golds in 1996, 2012, 2016, and 2024.

Eight American female gymnasts have won at least four medals at the Olympic Games the most of which was Simone Biles's tally of eleven total medal (including seven gold medals). Other top medalists include: Shannon Miller (seven), Sunisa Lee (six), Aly Raisman (six), Nastia Liukin (five), Mary Lou Retton (five), Dominique Dawes (four), and Shawn Johnson (four).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_female_artistic_gymnasts_for_the_United_States#cite_note-Miller-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_female_artistic_gymnasts_for_the_United_States#cite_note-Liukin-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_female_artistic_gymnasts_for_the_United_States#cite_note-Retton-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_female_artistic_gymnasts_for_the_United_States#cite_note-Dawes-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_female_artistic_gymnasts_for_the_United_States#cite_note-Johnson-7)
In 1984, Mary Lou Retton became the first American female gymnast to win the individual all-around gold medal at the Olympics.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_female_artistic_gymnasts_for_the_United_States#cite_note-8) She won five total medals that year in the only Olympic Games she participated in.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_female_artistic_gymnasts_for_the_United_States#cite_note-Retton-5)

Shannon Miller, who competed at the 1992 and 1996 Olympics, won seven total Olympic medals, which was the most of any American female gymnast before the 2021 Olympics in which Simone Biles tied for the number of Olympic medals won. Miller won five medals in 1992 and added two more in 1996.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_female_artistic_gymnasts_for_the_United_States#cite_note-gymnastics-9)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_female_artistic_gymnasts_for_the_United_States#cite_note-Miller-3) Dominique Dawes competed at the 1992, 1996, and 2000 Olympics, winning four medals.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_female_artistic_gymnasts_for_the_United_States#cite_note-Dawes-6) Miller and Dawes were both members of the "Magnificent Seven", the 1996 team that became the first American squad to win the team all-around gold medal at the Olympics. The competition was highlighted by Kerri Strug sticking a vault while injured to ensure the U.S. victory.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_female_artistic_gymnasts_for_the_United_States#cite_note-10)
Nastia Liukin and Shawn Johnson won five and four medals, respectively, in 2008, the only Olympics that either one participated in. Liukin won the individual all-around gold medal, and Johnson won the balance beam gold medal.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_female_artistic_gymnasts_for_the_United_States#cite_note-Liukin-4)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_female_artistic_gymnasts_for_the_United_States#cite_note-Johnson-7)

In 2012 the U.S. won the team gold medal for the second time. This team, which was nicknamed the "Fierce Five", featured five gymnasts who were all making their first appearance at the Olympics.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_female_artistic_gymnasts_for_the_United_States#cite_note-11) That year, Gabby Douglas won the gold medal in individual all-around, and Aly Raisman won the gold medal on floor exercise and the bronze medal on balance beam. McKayla Maroney won silver on vault.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_female_artistic_gymnasts_for_the_United_States#cite_note-Douglas-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_female_artistic_gymnasts_for_the_United_States#cite_note-Raisman-13)
In 2016 the U.S. won the team gold medal for the second consecutive Olympics, and the third title overall. The team was nicknamed "The Final Five" (as the team members were the last 5 who competed under Marta Karolyi) and featured the return of 2012 Olympic gold medalists Gabby Douglas and Aly Raisman. It also featured newcomers Laurie Hernandez, Madison Kocian, and three-time reigning world all-around champion Simone Biles. Biles won the individual all-around, vault, and floor exercise gold medals, and also took bronze on the balance beam. Raisman won silver medals in the all-around and floor exercise. Hernandez took the silver on the balance beam while Kocian, the reigning uneven bars world co-champion, won silver on that event. The 2016 Olympics were the most successful games to date for the United States in women's gymnastics, with four golds, four silvers, and one bronze medal overall.

For the 2020 Olympics (held in 2021 due to COVID-19), the U.S. women's team earned the team silver medal. Simone Biles was the only gymnast from the previous Olympics to return to the team. Sunisa Lee became the individual all-around champion, the sixth women from the U.S. to do so. Lee also won the bronze on uneven bars, Biles won bronze on balance beam, MyKayla Skinner won silver on Vault, and Jade Carey won gold on floor exercise.
Four U.S. Olympic gymnasts returned to the 2024 Olympics - Simone Biles, Jade Carey, Jordan Chiles and Sunisa Lee. In addition, 16 year old Hezly Rivera was chosen for the team. The five won the team all-around gold medal, while Biles and Lee won the gold and bronze individual all-around medals, respectively. Biles went on to win gold on vault and silver on floor exercise, while Lee won the bronze on uneven bars and Carey won bronze on vault.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
2012 Olympic Team, the "Fierce Five" at the White House
Gymnastics events have been staged at the Olympic Games since 1896,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_female_artistic_gymnasts_for_the_United_States#cite_note-1) but women's events first appeared in 1928. American female gymnasts have participated in every Olympic Games since 1936, except for 1980.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_female_artistic_gymnasts_for_the_United_States#cite_note-team-2) A total of 90 female gymnasts have represented the United States. American women have won 62 medals at the Olympics – 11 in team all-around, 11 in individual all-around, 7 in vault, 10 in uneven bars, 11 in balance beam, and 12 in floor exercise. The medals include 19 golds. The U.S. has medaled in the team all-around in every Summer Olympics since 1992, winning golds in 1996, 2012, 2016, and 2024.
texts.1:
Eight American female gymnasts have won at least four medals at the Olympic Games the most of which was Simone Biles's tally of eleven total medal (including seven gold medals). Other top medalists include: Shannon Miller (seven), Sunisa Lee (six), Aly Raisman (six), Nastia Liukin (five), Mary Lou Retton (five), Dominique Dawes (four), and Shawn Johnson (four).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_female_artistic_gymnasts_for_the_United_States#cite_note-Miller-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_female_artistic_gymnasts_for_the_United_States#cite_note-Liukin-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_female_artistic_gymnasts_for_the_United_States#cite_note-Retton-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_female_artistic_gymnasts_for_the_United_States#cite_note-Dawes-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_female_artistic_gymnasts_for_the_United_States#cite_note-Johnson-7)
In 1984, Mary Lou Retton became the first American female gymnast to win the individual all-around gold medal at the Olympics.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_female_artistic_gymnasts_for_the_United_States#cite_note-8) She won five total medals that year in the only Olympic Games she participated in.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_female_artistic_gymnasts_for_the_United_States#cite_note-Retton-5)
texts.2:
Shannon Miller, who competed at the 1992 and 1996 Olympics, won seven total Olympic medals, which was the most of any American female gymnast before the 2021 Olympics in which Simone Biles tied for the number of Olympic medals won. Miller won five medals in 1992 and added two more in 1996.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_female_artistic_gymnasts_for_the_United_States#cite_note-gymnastics-9)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_female_artistic_gymnasts_for_the_United_States#cite_note-Miller-3) Dominique Dawes competed at the 1992, 1996, and 2000 Olympics, winning four medals.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_female_artistic_gymnasts_for_the_United_States#cite_note-Dawes-6) Miller and Dawes were both members of the "Magnificent Seven", the 1996 team that became the first American squad to win the team all-around gold medal at the Olympics. The competition was highlighted by Kerri Strug sticking a vault while injured to ensure the U.S. victory.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_female_artistic_gymnasts_for_the_United_States#cite_note-10)
Nastia Liukin and Shawn Johnson won five and four medals, respectively, in 2008, the only Olympics that either one participated in. Liukin won the individual all-around gold medal, and Johnson won the balance beam gold medal.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_female_artistic_gymnasts_for_the_United_States#cite_note-Liukin-4)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_female_artistic_gymnasts_for_the_United_States#cite_note-Johnson-7)
texts.3:
In 2012 the U.S. won the team gold medal for the second time. This team, which was nicknamed the "Fierce Five", featured five gymnasts who were all making their first appearance at the Olympics.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_female_artistic_gymnasts_for_the_United_States#cite_note-11) That year, Gabby Douglas won the gold medal in individual all-around, and Aly Raisman won the gold medal on floor exercise and the bronze medal on balance beam. McKayla Maroney won silver on vault.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_female_artistic_gymnasts_for_the_United_States#cite_note-Douglas-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_female_artistic_gymnasts_for_the_United_States#cite_note-Raisman-13)
In 2016 the U.S. won the team gold medal for the second consecutive Olympics, and the third title overall. The team was nicknamed "The Final Five" (as the team members were the last 5 who competed under Marta Karolyi) and featured the return of 2012 Olympic gold medalists Gabby Douglas and Aly Raisman. It also featured newcomers Laurie Hernandez, Madison Kocian, and three-time reigning world all-around champion Simone Biles. Biles won the individual all-around, vault, and floor exercise gold medals, and also took bronze on the balance beam. Raisman won silver medals in the all-around and floor exercise. Hernandez took the silver on the balance beam while Kocian, the reigning uneven bars world co-champion, won silver on that event. The 2016 Olympics were the most successful games to date for the United States in women's gymnastics, with four golds, four silvers, and one bronze medal overall.

For the 2020 Olympics (held in 2021 due to COVID-19), the U.S. women's team earned the team silver medal. Simone Biles was the only gymnast from the previous Olympics to return to the team. Sunisa Lee became the individual all-around champion, the sixth women from the U.S. to do so. Lee also won the bronze on uneven bars, Biles won bronze on balance beam, MyKayla Skinner won silver on Vault, and Jade Carey won gold on floor exercise.
Four U.S. Olympic gymnasts returned to the 2024 Olympics - Simone Biles, Jade Carey, Jordan Chiles and Sunisa Lee. In addition, 16 year old Hezly Rivera was chosen for the team. The five won the team all-around gold medal, while Biles and Lee won the gold and bronze individual all-around medals, respectively. Biles went on to win gold on vault and silver on floor exercise, while Lee won the bronze on uneven bars and Carey won bronze on vault.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
